newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea cracks down on strike leaders.
newsitem.headline: South Korea cracks down on strike leaders.

text.p: South Korean state prosecutors on Monday summoned striking union leaders for questioning, setting up a showdown between the government and militant workers who have crippled key industries.
Senior prosecutor Lee Sang-hyong said about 20 leaders of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions were ordered to appear before prosecutors by Tuesday.

The government has declared unlawful strikes that have swept the nation since the government pushed a new labour law through parliament in a dawn session on December 26 with no debate and no opposition deputies present.
Unionists have demanded repeal of the law, which allows employers to lay off workers, eroding decades of near-total job security.
Lee said about 10 confederation leaders must report to the Seoul Prosecution Office and the others to local prosecutors responsible for provincial areas.
On Monday stoppages that have paralysed large sections of industry, including carmaking and shipbuilding, resumed after the New Year's holiday.

Production at Kia Motors was halted on Monday, but non-union workers and office staff were standing by to restart lines if it appeared that unions would extend their industrial action, a company official said.
Hyundai Motor Co Ltd and 12 other firms affiliated with South Korea's Hyundai Group were idled, a union official said.
"Hyundai Motor and the other unions were on indefinite strikes as of 8:30 a.m. (2330 GMT Sunday)," the official said. This affected 73,341 union workers.
Hyundai Group has 20 unions in total. Among the unions on strike were Hyundai Precision and Industry Co Ltd, Hyundai Motor Service Co Ltd and Hyundai Mipo Dock Yard Co Ltd.
But workers were keeping lines open at Daewoo Motors and Ssangyong Motors while union leaders met to discuss their next move, company officials said.
Stocks fell from the opening bell on news of the crackdown and fears that action against union leaders would further inflame industrial unrest.
"Worries that the strikes will intensify is really hurting sentiment," said broker Ha Young-hyun of Hyundai Securities. "I don't see much room for improvement at the moment."
Traders had said they expected strikes to ease after the confederation said on Sunday it would delay stoppages by some public-sector unions.
